module_title: Gibbs Free Energy, Entropy & Ionic Equilibrium Basics (Intermediate)
introduction: This level introduces the Second Law of Thermodynamics, focusing on entropy and the ultimate criterion for spontaneity: Gibbs Free Energy. It also transitions into Ionic Equilibrium, detailing acid-base theories, the pH scale, and the ionization of weak electrolytes.

core_concepts.title: Entropy ($\Delta S$) and Second Law of Thermodynamics
core_concepts.description: Entropy is a thermodynamic state function representing the degree of randomness or disorder in a system. $\Delta S = \frac{q_{\text{rev}}}{T}$. The Second Law states that for any spontaneous process, the total entropy of the universe (System + Surroundings) must increase: $\Delta S_{\text{univ}} > 0$. The Third Law states the entropy of a perfectly crystalline solid at absolute zero ($0 \text{ K}$) is zero.

core_concepts.title: Gibbs Free Energy ($\Delta G$) and Spontaneity
core_concepts.description:
Gibbs Free Energy combines enthalpy and entropy: $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$. It represents the maximum useful (non-expansion) work a system can do. 
- If $\Delta G < 0$: The process is Spontaneous.
- If $\Delta G > 0$: The process is Non-spontaneous.
- If $\Delta G = 0$: The system is at Equilibrium.

core_concepts.title: Thermodynamics of Equilibrium
core_concepts.description:
The relationship between standard Gibbs Free Energy change and the equilibrium constant is: $\Delta G^\circ = -RT \ln K = -2.303 RT \log_{10} K$. 
If $\Delta G^\circ$ is negative, $K > 1$ (products favored). If $\Delta G^\circ$ is positive, $K < 1$ (reactants favored). Note that at equilibrium, $\Delta G = 0$, but $\Delta G^\circ$ is a constant and is generally NOT zero.

core_concepts.title: Acid-Base Theories
core_concepts.description:
1. Arrhenius: Acids yield $H^+$ (or $H_3O^+$) in water; Bases yield $OH^-$ in water.
2. Brønsted-Lowry: Acids are Proton ($H^+$) donors; Bases are Proton ($H^+$) acceptors. Every acid forms a Conjugate Base (Acid minus $H^+$), and every base forms a Conjugate Acid (Base plus $H^+$).
3. Lewis: Acids are Electron-pair acceptors (Electrophiles); Bases are Electron-pair donors (Nucleophiles).

core_concepts.title: Ionic Product of Water ($K_w$) and pH Scale
core_concepts.description:
Water undergoes self-ionization: $H_2O \rightleftharpoons H^+ + OH^-$. The ionic product is $K_w = [H^+][OH^-]$. At $25^\circ\text{C}$ ($298 \text{ K}$), $K_w = 1.0 \times 10^{-14}$. 
The pH scale is logarithmic: $\text{pH} = -\log_{10}[H^+]$. Similarly, $\text{pOH} = -\log_{10}[OH^-]$. At $25^\circ\text{C}$, $\text{pH} + \text{pOH} = 14$.

important_entities.name: Ostwald's Dilution Law
important_entities.significance: The degree of dissociation ($\alpha$) of a weak electrolyte is inversely proportional to the square root of its concentration ($C$). Therefore, as a weak acid or base is diluted (concentration decreases), its degree of ionization INCREASES. At infinite dilution, even weak electrolytes behave like strong electrolytes ($\alpha \approx 1$).

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: A massive conceptual trap! The ionization of water is an endothermic process. If you heat water above $25^\circ\text{C}$ (e.g., to $90^\circ\text{C}$), more water molecules dissociate, increasing both $[H^+]$ and $[OH^-]$. Consequently, $K_w$ increases (e.g., to $10^{-12}$), and the pH of pure, neutral water DROPS below 7 (e.g., to 6). It is still chemically neutral because $[H^+] = [OH^-]$, but neutrality is no longer at pH 7.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: High T helps the positive; Low T helps the negative
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation:
To predict spontaneity from $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$:
- $\Delta H(-), \Delta S(+)$: Spontaneous at ALL temps.
- $\Delta H(+), \Delta S(-)$: Non-spontaneous at ALL temps.
- $\Delta H(+), \Delta S(+)$: Spontaneous only at HIGH temps ($T > \Delta H/\Delta S$).
- $\Delta H(-), \Delta S(-)$: Spontaneous only at LOW temps ($T < \Delta H/\Delta S$).

exam_strategy_tips: For finding the pH of very dilute strong acids (e.g., $10^{-8} \text{ M HCl}$), do NOT just take the negative log to get pH = 8 (acids cannot have a basic pH!). You MUST add the $[H^+]$ contribution from water ($10^{-7} \text{ M}$). The total $[H^+] = 10^{-8} + 10^{-7} = 1.1 \times 10^{-7}$, yielding a pH slightly less than 7 (approx 6.96).
